The percentage of residential parcels within a local jurisdiction that are located within a half-mile network distance of at least one outdoor public recreational facility is a key metric for assessing community access to recreational spaces. 2. Communities should enhance infrastructure that supports bicycling, such as increasing the total miles of designated shared-use paths and bike lanes relative to the total street miles (excluding limited-access highways) maintained by the local jurisdiction. 3. Communities should improve infrastructure that supports walking by increasing the total miles of paved sidewalks relative to the total street miles (excluding limited-access highways) maintained by the local jurisdiction. 4. Communities should support the placement of schools within easy walking distance of residential areas. 5. Communities should improve access to public transportation. 6. Communities should zone for mixed-use development, which combines residential land use with one or more commercial, institutional, or other public land uses. 7. Communities should enhance personal safety in areas where individuals are or could be physically active. This can be assessed by the number of vacant or abandoned buildings (residential and commercial) relative to the total number of buildings within a local jurisdiction. 8. Communities should enhance traffic safety in areas where individuals are or could be physically active. 9. Communities should actively participate in community coalitions or partnerships to address obesity. 10. For individuals to make healthy food choices, healthy food options must be available and accessible. Families living in low-income and minority neighborhoods often have less access to healthier food and beverage choices compared to those in higher-income areas. 11. Schools are a critical venue for increasing the availability of healthier foods and beverages for children. Other public service venues, such as after-school programs, childcare centers, community recreational facilities, parks, playgrounds, swimming pools, city and county buildings, prisons, and juvenile detention centers, also play a role in influencing the availability of healthier food options. 12. Improving the availability of healthier food and beverage choices, such as fruits, vegetables, and water, may increase the consumption of these healthier options. 13. The CDC's Community Guide reports insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of multicomponent school-based nutrition initiatives designed to increase fruit and vegetable intake and decrease fat and saturated fat intake among school-aged children. However, systematic research reviews have shown an association between the availability of fruits and vegetables and increased consumption. 14. Farm-to-school salad bar programs, which deliver produce from local farms to schools, have been shown to increase fruit and vegetable consumption among students. 15. A two-year randomized controlled trial of a school-based environmental intervention that increased the availability of lower-fat foods in cafeteria à la carte areas demonstrated that sales of lower-fat foods increased among adolescents attending schools exposed to the intervention. 16. A policy exists to apply nutrition standards consistent with the Dietary Guidelines for Americans to all food sold (e.g., meal menus and vending machines) within local government facilities or on public school campuses during the school day within the largest school district in a local jurisdiction. 17. 18. Healthier foods are generally more expensive than less healthy foods, which can pose a significant barrier to purchasing and consuming healthier options, particularly for low-income consumers. 19. Strategies to improve the affordability of healthier foods and beverages include lowering prices, providing discount coupons or vouchers redeemable for healthier foods, and offering bonuses tied to the purchase of healthier foods. 20. Pricing strategies create incentives for purchasing and consuming healthier foods and beverages by lowering the prices of such items relative to less healthy options. These strategies can be applied in public service venues, such as schools and recreation centers, by decreasing the prices of healthier foods sold in vending machines and cafeterias and increasing the prices of less healthy foods and beverages at concession stands. 21. Research has demonstrated that reducing the cost of healthier foods increases their purchase. For example, one study indicated that sales of fruits and carrots in high-school cafeterias increased when their prices were reduced.
